t: The Worst Mistake A Teacher Can Make
q: You see, the worst mistake you can make as a (caring) teacher is to make excuses for poor behavior.
Because as soon as you do, as soon as you start looking outside yourself for why your students are the way they are, you undermine your ability to do anything about it.
Taking responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom, on the other hand, is deeply empowering.
No doubt these factors exist, but they’re not insurmountable—not even close. In fact, we have yet to see or hear of a teaching situation we don’t firmly believe can be dramatically improved.
We receive dozens of emails from teachers every week who have put our simple strategies into practice and transformed their class.
You must never give in. You must never back down. You must never decide a student’s fate because of where they grow up, who their parents are, or how poorly they’re behaving in the moment.

t: Are You Focusing On The Wrong Students?
q: A second group of students would emerge from the mist. This group, numbering between six and eight, but occasionally more, are the real source of the problem.
They are the oxygen that fuels the incitement of the few. They are the poor role models, the laughers of jokes, and the creators of tension.
The truth is, your difficult students don’t need any extra time or attention from you.
This idea that one or two students are creating most, or all, of the trouble and misbehavior in your classroom is a fallacy.
From the first day of school onward you must teach, model, and require exceptional behavior from all students. You must lock it down and button it up.
As your happy crew gets larger and larger, and the feeling of being part of something special grows stronger and stronger, no one will be able to resist its gravitational pull.

t: Do You Need “Proof” To Hold Students Accountable? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/06/13/do-you-need-proof-to-hold-students-accountable/
q: But a couple years ago I received one from a teacher who wouldn’t hold students accountable unless he had what he described as “proof.
He did it because he was fearful that parents might not believe him. He was fearful they would take their child’s word over his own.
You are the teacher of the classroom. You are the leader tasked with shaping and inspiring your students and preparing them to be vital and contributing members of society.
Once you know the truth, you have an obligation to the misbehaving student, their parents, and to the rest of your class to hold them accountable.
Teachers who faithfully follow their classroom management plan with every student and in every situation receive far fewer complaints.
To be respected, admired, and trusted by students and parents alike, you must square your shoulders day after day and do what is right and what needs to be done.

t: A Trendy Classroom Management Strategy You Should Never Use you-should-never-use/
q: It’s a close cousin of the “caught being good” strategy, which we also don’t recommend, but is far more damaging to the targeted student.
You would give the students within proximity of the misbehaving student an enthusiastic pat on the back for not misbehaving.
It’s the classroom management version of a magician’s sleight of hand. But it’s cruel and dishonest and doesn’t help the student actually change their behavior.
It will make difficult students less inclined to get back on track in the future and turn your classroom into a petri dish of neediness, dependency, and underachievement.
Have a classroom management plan that clearly lays out the rules and consequences of the class.
What they really need is your honesty. They need your truth and forgiveness. They need your accountability, your leadership, and your consistency.
